sections.h2: Where is Simsbury, CT, and what is the setting?
sections.html:
Simsbury is a town in Hartford County at the northern end of the Farmington Valley, with a 2020 census population of 24,517. It covers about 34.3 square miles and belongs to the Capitol Planning Region.

The Farmington River runs through town. Talcott Mountain, part of the Metacomet Ridge, flanks the east side, and Heublein Tower, Talcott Mountain State Park, Penwood State Park and the Tariffville Gorge are all along that ridge. The Pinchot Sycamore, the largest tree in Connecticut, grows near the river. Belden Forest, a 40-acre old-growth tract near the town center, joined the Old-Growth Forest Network in 2019.

Homes close to the river, the ridge and the state parks draw their own kinds of buyers.

Simsbury was incorporated on May 12, 1670, as Connecticut's 21st town, on land the Massaco band had lived on. Settlers from Windsor came in the 1660s.

In March 1676, during King Philip's War, the town was pillaged and burned, and settlers stayed in Windsor until spring 1677. The area later split into Granby in 1786 and Canton in 1806. On December 20, 1859, the Patent Safety Fuse factory near the town center exploded and killed eight people. Ensign-Bickford, founded in Simsbury in 1836, is still headquartered in town.

The population was 4,822 in 1950 and 10,138 in 1960, then 17,475 in 1970. Much of the housing came with that postwar jump, with older homes in the historic districts.

sections.h2: Which Simsbury villages and districts matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Simsbury has four census-designated places: Simsbury Center, Tariffville, Weatogue and West Simsbury. Early resettled communities were East Weatogue, Simsbury Center and Terry's Plain.

  • Simsbury Center Historic District: Hopmeadow Street from West Street to Massaco Street, listed in 1996.
  • Tariffville Historic District: listed in 1993.
  • Terry's Plain Historic District: listed in 1993.
  • East Weatogue Historic District: listed in 1990, including the c. 1760 John Humphrey House.

Several historic districts are listed on the National Register. A National Register listing does not by itself set local rules, so ask the town whether your property has local restrictions before you plan exterior work.

sections.h2: What historic buildings are in Simsbury Center?
sections.html:
Simsbury Center has a cluster of National Register buildings along Hopmeadow Street. They include the Phelps Tavern Museum and Homestead at 800 Hopmeadow Street, a 1771 house used as a tavern from 1786 to 1849, and Eno Memorial Hall at 754 Hopmeadow Street.

  • Simsbury Townhouse at 695 Hopmeadow Street, the original town hall in the Greek Revival style, first built in 1839.
  • Robert and Julia Darling House at 720 Hopmeadow Street.
  • Simsbury Bank and Trust Company Building at 760 to 762 Hopmeadow Street.
  • Horace Belden School at 933 Hopmeadow Street, now the Town Hall and police station.

The Town Hall sits in that historic stretch, so it is a convenient first stop for permit, assessment and land records questions. The Drake Hill Road Bridge, a pin-connected Parker truss built in 1892 over the Farmington River, is open to foot and bicycle traffic and is one of three surviving Parker trusses in Connecticut.

Simsbury's top employer in the 2024 annual financial report is the Board of Education, with 651 employees, followed by several private companies. The report also lists Ensign-Bickford, Wings Media Group, Everest Global Services, Chubb, Keller Williams Realty, Hoffman Auto Group, McLean Home Care, The Hartford and Stop and Shop.

  • Simsbury Board of Education: 651
  • Ensign-Bickford, Wings Media Group, Everest Global: each in the 500 to 999 range
  • Chubb, Keller Williams Realty, Hoffman Auto Group, McLean Home Care: each in the 250 to 499 range

Many residents commute within greater Hartford, so job changes in insurance and related fields can drive a move.

Simsbury more than doubled in the 1950s and nearly doubled again in the 1960s, then slowed. Growth between 2000 and 2010 was 1.2 percent, and between 2010 and 2020 it was 4.3 percent. A town that grew that fast in two decades has many houses from the 1950s through 1970s, and sellers of those homes often weigh how much to spend on updates before listing.

Simsbury Public Schools includes Simsbury High School, Henry James Memorial School for grades 7 and 8, and the elementary schools Central, Latimer Lane, Squadron Line, Tariffville and Tootin' Hills. Private options include the Ethel Walker School, Westminster School, The Master's School, St. Mary's School and the Cobb School Montessori.

Buyers often ask which elementary school serves a house, so have your attendance zone ready.

sections.h2: What does the weather mean for a Simsbury home?
sections.html:
Simsbury receives about 46 inches of precipitation in a year, with record temperatures from 102 degrees down to minus 26. January averages a daily high of 34 and a low of 18.

Roofs, heating systems and pipes are the usual winter concerns. Homes near the Farmington River should check flood zone status through the town before listing, since lenders look at it. Ask the town for local flood maps rather than assuming either way.

sections.h2: How is a Simsbury sale recorded and taxed?
sections.html:
The seller files Connecticut Form OP-236 with the Simsbury town clerk when the deed is recorded, and tax is due once the price reaches two thousand dollars, unless an exemption applies.

  • One exemption covers a principal residence with a crumbling foundation caused by pyrrhotite, as determined by a professional engineer. It applies only to the first transfer after the written evaluation and needs a copy of that report attached.
  • A deed in lieu of foreclosure on a principal residence is also exempt.
  • Estates and trusts that sell attach Schedule A.

Rates change, so ask your closing attorney for the current numbers. For tax bills, ask the Simsbury assessor and tax collector.

sections.h2: What do sellers in Simsbury usually face?
sections.html:
Simsbury sellers usually face an older house, a decision about repairs or a relocation. The town's mix of historic village homes and postwar houses means condition varies a lot.

  • Repairs: get an estimate before comparing a repaired listing with an as-is sale.
  • Foundation concerns: Connecticut has a specific exemption for pyrrhotite damage, so ask an engineer if you suspect it.
  • Estate or divorce: confirm legal authority to sell first.

A cash offer lets you sell the house as it stands, and you can decline.

faqs.a: Simsbury was incorporated on May 12, 1670, as Connecticut's 21st town.

faqs.q: How many people live in Simsbury?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 24,517 residents in a town of about 34.3 square miles.

faqs.q: What are the largest employers in Simsbury?
faqs.a: The Board of Education leads with 651 employees, followed by Ensign-Bickford, Wings Media Group, Everest Global and Chubb.

faqs.q: Is there an exemption for pyrrhotite foundations when selling?
faqs.a: Yes. Connecticut exempts the first transfer of a principal residence with a deteriorating concrete foundation, as determined by a professional engineer, from the state conveyance tax, with the engineer's report attached.

Simsbury Town Hall and the police station are in the former Horace Belden School at 933 Hopmeadow Street. Call ahead to confirm hours and which office handles your question about assessment, permits or land records.
Simsbury High School is the public high school, at 34 Farms Village Road, with 1,457 students listed.
